# Data Wrangling Essentials {#sec-wrangling}

```{r}
#| label: wrangling-opening
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")
opening_sbp <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site))) |>
  summarize(sbp = mean(sbp_discharge, na.rm = TRUE), .by = site)
opening_d <- round(opening_sbp$sbp[opening_sbp$site == "Site D"], 1)
opening_others <- round(
  range(opening_sbp$sbp[opening_sbp$site != "Site D"]), 1
)
```

The HF-HOME case report form (CRF) export arrives from five
hospitals, and each wrote its own conventions into the file. Read
it with the defaults, summarize systolic blood pressure at
discharge by site, and Site D's mean is `r opening_d` mmHg against
`r opening_others[1]` to `r opening_others[2]` at the other four:
a site difference large enough to earn a sentence in the methods
section and a covariate in the model. Nothing in the patients
supports it. Site D writes a missing measurement as `-99`, the
default read accepted it as a pressure, and the mean did what
means do. Every decision a cleaning script makes (what a code
means, which rows are excluded, which of two conflicting values
survives) is a decision about what the analysis is of, made before
any model and rarely questioned afterward. This chapter makes
those decisions in code, where a reader can see them and count
what each one did.

::: {.bookepigraph}

```

messy in its own way.*

library(tidyverse)
```

**You'll be able to.**

- Read a raw export so that every missing-value code and site
  convention stays visible until you decide what it means.
- Recode per-site conventions (sex codes, date formats, missing
  codes) and verify each recode with a cross-tabulation.
- Choose the long or wide shape for the operation at hand, and
  find the duplicates that make a pivot fail.

## Reading the export deliberately {#sec-wrangling-reading}

The `dplyr` and `tidyr` verbs take an afternoon to learn, and this
chapter does not re-teach them.[^r4ds] What takes longer is
deciding what the values mean, and that decision starts at the
read. The raw-data rule of @sec-acquisition applies throughout:
`crf_export.csv` is evidence, never edited, and everything the
script produces is written somewhere else (Habit 2).

[^r4ds]: The generic tour of `filter()`, `select()`, `mutate()`,
    `summarize()`, and `arrange()` is R for Data Science
    [@wickham2023r4ds, chs. 3 and 5]. Readers coming from `pandas`
    will find that the verbs map closely onto `query()`,
    `assign()`, and `groupby().agg()`.

### What the defaults guessed

`readr` guesses a type for every column from its first rows. The
guesses are usually right about the type and silent about the
meaning.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-default-read
library(tidyverse)
hf_dir <- file.path("..", "data", "raw_data", "hfhome")

crf_default <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                        show_col_types = FALSE)
spec(crf_default)

crf_default |>
  summarize(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_discharge, na.rm = TRUE),
            n = n(), .by = site) |>
  arrange(site)
```

The summary has two problems before it has any results: fifteen
spellings of five sites, and a Site D mean several points below
the rest. Neither raised a message.

### Read everything as text first

A first read for discovery keeps every value as text and turns off
`readr`'s own idea of what is missing, so that the empty strings,
the `NA` strings, and the `-99` all arrive as written and can be
counted.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-raw-read
crf_raw <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv"),
                    col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
                    na = character())
crf_raw |> count(sex)
```

The missing-value codes are a finding, so tabulate them by site.
Pivoting the three numeric columns into one makes that a single
`count()`:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-missing-codes
crf_raw |>
  mutate(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(ef_pct, sbp_discharge, weight_kg),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(value %in% c("", "NA", "-99")) |>
  count(site, value)
```

Each site uses one convention: an empty field at A and C, the
string `NA` at B and E, and `-99` at D. Reading as text is Habit 7
in practice: nothing is converted until you have decided what each
value means.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A missing-value code that parses as a number becomes data.**
`-99` is a valid double, so the default read stored it as one, and
`na.rm = TRUE` removed only the true `NA`s. No type check knows
that a systolic pressure cannot be negative. Name the codes when
you convert (`parse_double(x, na = c("", "NA", "-99"))`) and then
assert the plausible range, so that the next unannounced code
stops the script.
:::

### Exercises

1. For each site, count the missing-value codes in
   `sbp_discharge` and in `weight_kg` separately. Then confirm
   that the totals equal the number of missing values in the
   clean `baseline.csv`, which the running study supplies as an
   answer key.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-13-1
missing_codes <- crf_raw |>
  mutate(site = str_to_title(str_squish(site))) |>
  pivot_longer(c(sbp_discharge, weight_kg),
               names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(value %in% c("", "NA", "-99")) |>
  count(variable, site, value)
missing_codes

baseline <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "baseline.csv"),
                     col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                     show_col_types = FALSE)
totals <- missing_codes |> summarize(n = sum(n), .by = variable)
stopifnot(
  totals$n[totals$variable == "sbp_discharge"] ==
    sum(is.na(baseline$sbp_discharge)),
  totals$n[totals$variable == "weight_kg"] ==
    sum(is.na(baseline$weight_kg))
)
totals
```

The two totals match the clean table, so the three codes are the
only ones in use. A real export has no answer key; the equivalent
check is the plausible-range assertion after conversion.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Why read every column as character, with `na =
character()`, instead of passing the right `na` codes to
`read_csv()` from the start?

**Answer.** Because you do not know the codes until you have
looked, and an assumed list hides the ones you did not assume. The
text read lets you count every code by site, which is how you
learn that only Site D uses `-99`. Once the codes are known, naming
them in the conversion step records the decision in code. A single
`na =` list passed to `read_csv()` also applies to every column,
including identifiers and free text, where a string such as `NA`
might be a value.
:::

## Recoding site conventions {#sec-wrangling-recode}

Each site's convention is reasonable on its own. The script's job
is to map all five onto one, and to prove that the mapping did
what you meant.

### Labels and identifiers

Site labels vary in case and spacing; `str_squish()` removes the
stray spaces and `str_to_title()` fixes the case. Site E's system
dropped the leading zeros of `r sum(nchar(crf_raw$patient_id) < 4)`
patient IDs, which `str_pad()` restores. @sec-acquisition explains
how the zeros were lost, and @sec-joins what they cost at the
join.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-labels
crf_labeled <- crf_raw |>
  mutate(
    site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)),
    patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0")
  )
crf_labeled |> count(site)
```

This export's header is already in `snake_case`. Most are not, and
`janitor::clean_names()` is the one-line fix for headers such as
`Patient ID` or `SBP at Baseline (mmHg)`.

### Sex: a code means what the codebook says

Four sites write a letter or a word; Site D writes a number. The
recode below names every accepted spelling and leaves anything
else as `NA`, so that an unexpected code is caught by the
assertion rather than absorbed.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-sex
crf_sex <- crf_labeled |>
  mutate(
    sex_raw = sex,
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("F", "Female", "f") ~ "F",
      sex %in% c("M", "Male", "m") ~ "M",
      site == "Site D" & sex == "2" ~ "F",
      site == "Site D" & sex == "1" ~ "M"
    )
  )
stopifnot(!anyNA(crf_sex$sex))
crf_sex |> count(site, sex_raw, sex)
```

The cross-tabulation is the verification: every raw code appears
once, beside the value it became, and a reader can check each row
against the site's codebook.

::: {.callout-warning title='Pitfall'}
**A numeric sex code recoded from memory produces no `NA` and no
warning.** Site D's codebook says 1 is male and 2 is female, the
convention of ISO/IEC 5218; other systems number them the other
way. A recode written from habit rather than from the codebook
swaps the sex of all `r sum(crf_sex$site == "Site D")` Site D
patients, and every sex-specific result downstream is plausible
and wrong. Write the mapping from the codebook, and keep the raw
column until the cross-tabulation has been checked.
:::

### Dates: one format per site

The five sites write dates in four formats. Because each site is
internally consistent, the safe parse is per site:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-dates
parse_site_date <- function(x, site) {
  case_when(
    site %in% c("Site A", "Site B", "Site E") ~ ymd(x, quiet = TRUE),
    site == "Site C" ~ mdy(x, quiet = TRUE),
    site == "Site D" ~ dmy(x, quiet = TRUE)
  )
}

crf_dates <- crf_sex |>
  mutate(across(c(dob, discharge_date),
                \(x) parse_site_date(x, site)))
stopifnot(!anyNA(crf_dates$dob), !anyNA(crf_dates$discharge_date),
          all(crf_dates$dob < crf_dates$discharge_date))
range(crf_dates$discharge_date)
```

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-dates-lazy
#| include: false
lazy_dates <- as.Date(parse_date_time(
  crf_raw$discharge_date, orders = c("ymd", "mdy", "dmy"),
  quiet = TRUE
))
lazy_wrong <- which(lazy_dates != crf_dates$discharge_date)
```

The tempting alternative is one call to
`lubridate::parse_date_time()` with a list of orders. On this file
it returns a date for every row, and `r length(lazy_wrong)` of them
are wrong: Site D's `r crf_raw$discharge_date[lazy_wrong[1]]`
becomes `r format(lazy_dates[lazy_wrong[1]])`. @sec-types takes up
why ambiguous formats misparse and how to detect it.

### Numbers: name the codes, then check the range

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-numbers
crf_clean <- crf_dates |>
  mutate(across(c(ef_pct, sbp_discharge, weight_kg),
                \(x) parse_double(x, na = c("", "NA", "-99"))))
stopifnot(
  all(between(crf_clean$ef_pct, 5, 90)),
  all(between(crf_clean$sbp_discharge, 50, 250), na.rm = TRUE),
  all(between(crf_clean$weight_kg, 30, 250), na.rm = TRUE)
)
crf_clean |>
  summarize(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_discharge, na.rm = TRUE), .by = site)
```

Site D's mean now sits with the others. The range check is an
assertion, not a filter: when it fails, query the site and record
the answer, rather than dropping the row. Where a protocol does
exclude values, 'removed implausible values' is not a documented
rule; 'removed SBP above 250 or below 50', with the number and
percentage of patients computed by the script beside it, is.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
The running study ships the clean tables the export was written
from, so you can check the recodes against an answer key that a
real export would not have.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-recode-verify
demographics <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "demographics.csv"),
                         col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                         show_col_types = FALSE)
key <- match(crf_clean$patient_id, demographics$patient_id)
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(key),
  identical(crf_clean$sex, demographics$sex[key]),
  identical(crf_clean$dob, demographics$dob[key])
)
```

The chunk prints nothing when every patient's sex and date of birth
agree with the clean table.
:::

### Exercises

2. Reverse the Site D mapping (1 as female, 2 as male), and count
   how many patients then disagree with `demographics.csv`. Which
   check in the chapter would have caught the error without the
   answer key?
3. Parse `discharge_date` with
   `parse_date_time(orders = c("mdy", "dmy", "ymd"))` instead of
   per site. How many dates differ from the per-site parse, and at
   which sites?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-13-2
reversed <- crf_labeled |>
  mutate(sex = case_when(
    sex %in% c("F", "Female", "f") ~ "F",
    sex %in% c("M", "Male", "m") ~ "M",
    site == "Site D" & sex == "1" ~ "F",
    site == "Site D" & sex == "2" ~ "M"
  ))
sum(reversed$sex != demographics$sex[key])
```

Every Site D patient disagrees, and nothing else in the script
notices: there is no `NA`, so the `stopifnot()` passes. Only the
cross-tabulation read against the codebook catches it, which is why
the codebook, not memory, is the source of the mapping.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-13-3
other_order <- as.Date(parse_date_time(
  crf_raw$discharge_date, orders = c("mdy", "dmy", "ymd"),
  quiet = TRUE
))
differs <- other_order != crf_dates$discharge_date
sum(is.na(other_order))
crf_dates |> filter(differs) |> count(site)
```

Changing the order of the formats does not help: every date parses,
none is `NA`, and the same Site D dates land on the wrong day.
A parser that always returns a date cannot tell you it guessed.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** Next month Site B begins exporting `Unknown` for
sex. What does the recode in this section do, and what would a
recode written as `if_else(sex %in% c("M", "Male", "m"), "M",
"F")` do?

**Answer.** The `case_when()` above has no `.default`, so
`Unknown` becomes `NA` and `stopifnot(!anyNA(sex))` halts the
script, which is the loud failure you want. The `if_else()` version
assigns `F` to every value that is not a spelling of male, so
`Unknown` silently becomes female. Listing what each value means,
and refusing everything else, is what makes a new code visible.
:::

## Shapes: tidy, long, and wide {#sec-wrangling-shapes}

::: {.column-margin}
![Hadley Wickham, author of the tidyverse and of the tidy-data
formulation this chapter teaches. Photograph by Hadley Wickham,
[CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/),
via Wikimedia Commons.](images/portraits/wickham.jpg){fig-alt='Portrait
photograph of Hadley Wickham.'}
:::

Wickham's three rules [@wickham2014tidy] define tidy data, and the
HF-HOME files break each of them somewhere
(@tbl-tidy-rules).

| Rule | Broken when | HF-HOME example |
|---|---|---|
| Each variable forms a column | A value is stored in a column name | A lab table with `ntprobnp_d0` and `ntprobnp_d30`: visit is a variable hidden in the names |
| Each observation forms a row | One observation spans rows, or one row holds several | `labs.csv` records one discharge potassium twice, with different values |
| Each type of observational unit forms a table | Properties of different units share a table | `labs.csv` repeats `unit` on every row, though the unit belongs to the test, not to the measurement |

: Wickham's tidy-data rules and where the running study breaks
them. {#tbl-tidy-rules}

Tidy is not the goal; a correct analysis is. The long form is
usually the path to it, and the operation decides the shape.

### Long to wide, and the duplicate that stops it

`labs.csv` is long: one row per visit and test. A per-patient
table of discharge labs needs it wide, one row per patient and one
column per test. Visit `-01` is always the discharge visit.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-pivot-warning
#| warning: true
labs <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "labs.csv"),
                 col_types = cols(patient_id = col_character()),
                 show_col_types = FALSE)
discharge_labs <- labs |> filter(str_ends(visit_id, "-01"))

discharge_labs |>
  select(patient_id, test_code, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = test_code, values_from = value) |>
  filter(patient_id %in% c("0373", "2113"))
```

`pivot_wider()` warns and returns list-columns, because two
patient-test pairs have two values each. Count the keys before the
pivot, as @sec-joins counts them before a join:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-pivot-duplicates
dup_keys <- discharge_labs |>
  count(patient_id, test_code) |>
  filter(n > 1)
discharge_labs |> semi_join(dup_keys, by = c("patient_id", "test_code"))
```

One is an exact duplicate, which `distinct()` removes without
loss. The other is a potassium re-run with a different value, and
no rule in the data says which result stands. Supplying
`values_fn = mean` would silence the warning by inventing a value
nobody measured. Set the pair aside as a data query, and let the
patient's potassium be missing until the site answers:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-pivot-resolve
labs_distinct <- discharge_labs |> distinct()
lab_queries <- labs_distinct |>
  filter(n() > 1, .by = c(patient_id, test_code))
discharge_wide <- labs_distinct |>
  filter(n() == 1, .by = c(patient_id, test_code)) |>
  select(patient_id, test_code, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = test_code, values_from = value)

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(discharge_wide$patient_id))
lab_queries
nrow(discharge_wide)
```

The wide table has `r format(nrow(discharge_wide), big.mark = ",")` rows for
`r format(nrow(crf_clean), big.mark = ",")` randomized patients.
The extra one is an orphan lab record that @sec-joins catches with
an anti-join.

### The operation decides the shape

A per-test summary wants the long form, where test is a column to
group by:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-long-summary
labs_distinct |>
  summarize(median = median(value), q1 = quantile(value, 0.25),
            q3 = quantile(value, 0.75), n = n(), .by = test_code)
```

A condition that combines tests within a patient (low sodium *and*
abnormal potassium) wants the wide form, where both values sit in
one row. A trajectory plot wants long again, with visit as a
column to map to the x-axis (@sec-graphics). Pivot when the
operation requires it, not as a ritual; on a large file, a long
table is many times the size of the wide one.

### Writing your own verbs

A helper that takes a column name needs one of two idioms. Embrace
it with `{{ }}` when the caller types the name bare, and use
`.data[[ ]]` when the caller passes a string:

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-tidy-eval
count_by <- function(df, var) {
  df |> count({{ var }})
}
count_by_name <- function(df, var_name) {
  df |> count(.data[[var_name]])
}

count_by(crf_clean, site)
count_by_name(crf_clean, "sex")
```

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question 1.** `labs.csv` repeats `unit` on every row. Which tidy
rule does that bend, and is it worth fixing?

**Answer.** Rule 3. The unit is a property of the test: N-terminal
pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is in pg/mL for every
patient, so the unit belongs in a lookup table keyed by
`test_code`, and repeating it on every row is duplication that can
drift. Many analysts leave it in place and accept the risk, which
is a defensible choice when it is made deliberately and checked
(`count(labs, test_code, unit)` should give one row per test).

**Question 2.** What does `count_by(crf_clean, "site")`, with the
name passed as a string, return?

**Answer.** One row, with the literal string `"site"` as its value
and every patient counted in it. `{{ }}` embraces whatever it is
given, and a string is a constant, so the function counts by a
constant. There is no error, and the result has the right shape
with a meaningless number in it. `count_by_name(crf_clean, "site")`
is the string version; the rule is that `{{ }}` takes what the
caller types and `.data[[ ]]` takes a name your code computed.
:::

### Exercises

4. Using `discharge_wide`, count the patients whose discharge
   potassium is outside 3.5 to 5.0 mmol/L, the patients whose
   sodium is below 135 mmol/L, and the patients with both. Why
   does this question need the wide shape?

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-13-4
discharge_wide |>
  summarize(
    potassium_abnormal = sum(K < 3.5 | K > 5.0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sodium_low = sum(SODIUM < 135, na.rm = TRUE),
    both = sum((K < 3.5 | K > 5.0) & SODIUM < 135, na.rm = TRUE),
    potassium_missing = sum(is.na(K))
  )
```

The condition compares two tests for the same patient, so both
values must sit in one row. In the long form it needs a grouped
filter across rows, which is harder to read and easier to get
wrong. The one patient with a missing potassium is the queried
re-run; `na.rm = TRUE` leaves that patient out of the counts, which
the `potassium_missing` column makes visible rather than silent.
:::

## Worked example: from CRF export to derived baseline {#sec-wrangling-worked}

The script below is the chapter in one place: it reads the export
as text, recodes each site's conventions, asserts the result, adds
derived variables, counts what each filter removes, and writes the
derived data to its own directory. It reuses `parse_site_date()`
from @sec-wrangling-recode.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-worked-example
raw_path <- file.path(hf_dir, "crf_export.csv")
raw_md5 <- unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path))

baseline_derived <- read_csv(
  raw_path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
  na = character()
) |>
  mutate(
    site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)),
    patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0"),
    sex = case_when(
      sex %in% c("F", "Female", "f") ~ "F",
      sex %in% c("M", "Male", "m") ~ "M",
      site == "Site D" & sex == "2" ~ "F",
      site == "Site D" & sex == "1" ~ "M"
    ),
    across(c(dob, discharge_date), \(x) parse_site_date(x, site)),
    across(c(ef_pct, sbp_discharge, weight_kg),
           \(x) parse_double(x, na = c("", "NA", "-99"))),
    age = as.integer(floor(time_length(
      interval(dob, discharge_date), "years"
    ))),
    age_group = cut(age, breaks = c(-Inf, 65, 80, Inf), right = FALSE,
                    labels = c("under 65", "65 to 79", "80 or older"))
  )

randomized <- read_csv(file.path(hf_dir, "randomization.csv"),
                       col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
                       show_col_types = FALSE)

stopifnot(
  !anyDuplicated(baseline_derived$patient_id),
  !anyNA(baseline_derived$sex),
  !anyNA(baseline_derived$discharge_date),
  all(between(baseline_derived$ef_pct, 5, 90))
)

# one rule per step, so that each step's exclusions can be counted
on_list    <- baseline_derived |>
  filter(patient_id %in% randomized$patient_id)
with_sbp   <- on_list |> filter(!is.na(sbp_discharge))
with_vitals <- with_sbp |> filter(!is.na(weight_kg))

flow <- tibble(
  step = c("rows in the CRF export", "on the randomization list",
           "discharge SBP recorded", "discharge weight recorded"),
  n = c(nrow(baseline_derived), nrow(on_list), nrow(with_sbp),
        nrow(with_vitals))
) |>
  mutate(removed = lag(n) - n)
flow

derived_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "derived_data")
dir.create(derived_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_rds(baseline_derived, file.path(derived_dir, "crf_baseline.rds"))
write_csv(flow, file.path(derived_dir, "crf_flow.csv"))
```

The flow table answers a reviewer's first question about any
subset, which is how many patients each rule removed and why. In a
compendium, `derived_dir` is `analysis/data/derived_data/`
(@sec-rrtools); the chunk writes to a temporary directory so that
rendering the book leaves the repository unchanged.

Two judgments in the script belong to the analysis rather than to
the code. First, the flow does not define the analysis population.
HF-HOME is analyzed as randomized, so the primary analysis includes
all `r format(nrow(on_list), big.mark = ",")` patients on the
list. The last two steps describe the subset with complete vital
signs that a covariate-adjusted sensitivity analysis would use, and
reporting its
`r format(nrow(on_list) - nrow(with_vitals), big.mark = ",")`
exclusions is what lets a reader judge it. @sec-missing explains
why dropping them is not a neutral act.

Second, `age_group` is derived *beside* `age`, not in place of it.
Grouping age is a legitimate display choice for a table of
baseline characteristics. It is rarely a legitimate modeling
choice: categorizing a continuous predictor discards the variation
within each group, assumes a step function where the biology is
smooth, and makes the estimate depend on cutpoints that were chosen
rather than measured [@harrell2025bbr, ch. 18; @harrell2015rms].
Deriving `age_group` is cheap; recovering `age` after you have
overwritten it is not.

::: {.callout-tip title='Verification'}
Confirm that the derived file round-trips exactly, that the raw
file is byte-for-byte what it was before the script ran, and that
the derived ages agree with the clean table.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-worked-verify
stopifnot(
  identical(read_rds(file.path(derived_dir, "crf_baseline.rds")),
            baseline_derived),
  unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path)) == raw_md5,
  identical(baseline_derived$age,
            as.integer(demographics$age[key]))
)
```

An `.rds` file keeps types, dates, and factor levels that a
derived CSV would lose. The checksum is Habit 2 made executable:
the script read the evidence and did not touch it.
:::

::: {.callout-important title='LLM prompt'}
An agentic version: a coding agent writes and runs the recode, and
you review the evidence it reports. HF-HOME is synthetic, so the
agent may run against it; on a real export it would see the
codebook and synthetic rows only.

> **Context.** `analysis/data/raw_data/hfhome/crf_export.csv` is a
> raw CRF export from five sites; `README.md` in the same directory
> is the codebook and lists each site's sex coding, date format,
> and missing-value codes. Write `R/derive_baseline.R`.
>
> **Constraints.** Use `readr`, `dplyr`, `stringr`, and
> `lubridate`; add no packages. Read every column as character
> with `na = character()`. Never write to `raw_data/`. Map each
> code exactly as the codebook states, with no `.default` in any
> recode. Do not use `parse_date_time()` with several orders, and
> do not drop rows.
>
> **Criteria.** Before writing code, list each mapping you will
> apply and the codebook line it comes from. After running, report
> `count(site, sex_raw, sex)`, the missing codes found per site and
> column, the number of `NA` dates (which must be zero), and the
> row count in and out (which must be equal). If any assertion
> fails, stop and report it instead of fixing it.

*Failure mode.* The agent maps Site D's 1 and 2 from a convention
it has seen elsewhere, or converts the numeric columns with
`as.numeric()`, so that `-99` survives as a value; both pass every
structural check. *Check.* Read the cross-tabulation against the
codebook line by line, compare per-site means of `sbp_discharge`,
and search the diff for `as.numeric(`, `.default`, and
`parse_date_time(`. The governance rules are in
@sec-ai-governance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Check'}
**Question.** A reviewer asks why the primary analysis includes
`r format(nrow(on_list), big.mark = ",")` patients when the flow
table ends at `r format(nrow(with_vitals), big.mark = ",")`. What
do you answer?

**Answer.** The flow table describes a subset, not the analysis
population. The trial is analyzed as randomized, so every
randomized patient is in the primary analysis whether or not a
discharge vital sign was recorded; excluding patients by a
post-randomization measurement would break the comparison that
randomization created. The subset with complete vital signs serves
a sensitivity analysis, and the table reports what it lost.
:::

## Rules of thumb

1. **Habit 2: raw data are evidence; derived data are a build
   product.** Read the export, never write to it, and save what
   you derive to its own directory, with a checksum to prove it.
2. **Habit 7: convert late, validate early.** Read as text, count
   the codes, then convert with the codes named and the ranges
   asserted.
3. **Habit 8: a bug that produces a plausible number is the
   expensive kind.** A swapped code or a parsed `-99` raises
   nothing; a cross-tabulation and a range check make it loud.

## Cumulative practice

5. *Cumulative (uses @sec-acquisition).* Turn the worked example
   into a function, `derive_baseline(raw_path, out_dir)`, that
   writes the derived `.rds` and the flow table and returns the
   raw file's checksum. Call it twice into two directories and
   verify that the two derived files are identical and that the
   raw checksum did not change.
6. *On your own work (no key).* Take a raw export from your own
   work, or one in a public repository, and write the missing-code
   table and the recode cross-tabulations of this chapter for it.
   Record every decision you made that the codebook did not
   determine.

::: {.callout-note collapse='true' title='Solution to exercise 5'}
```{r}
#| label: soln-13-5
derive_baseline <- function(raw_path, out_dir) {
  dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  derived <- read_csv(
    raw_path, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()),
    na = character()
  ) |>
    mutate(
      site = str_to_title(str_squish(site)),
      patient_id = str_pad(patient_id, width = 4, pad = "0"),
      across(c(dob, discharge_date), \(x) parse_site_date(x, site)),
      across(c(ef_pct, sbp_discharge, weight_kg),
             \(x) parse_double(x, na = c("", "NA", "-99")))
    )
  flow <- tibble(
    step = c("rows in the CRF export", "discharge SBP recorded"),
    n = c(nrow(derived), sum(!is.na(derived$sbp_discharge)))
  )
  write_rds(derived, file.path(out_dir, "crf_baseline.rds"))
  write_csv(flow, file.path(out_dir, "crf_flow.csv"))
  unname(tools::md5sum(raw_path))
}

run_1 <- file.path(tempdir(), "run-1")
run_2 <- file.path(tempdir(), "run-2")
md5_1 <- derive_baseline(raw_path, run_1)
md5_2 <- derive_baseline(raw_path, run_2)

stopifnot(
  md5_1 == md5_2,
  unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(run_1, "crf_baseline.rds"))) ==
    unname(tools::md5sum(file.path(run_2, "crf_baseline.rds")))
)
```

The sex recode is left out to keep the key short; add it, with its
assertion, in your own version. Comparing the derived files by
checksum is stricter than comparing the data frames: it fails if
anything about the serialization changes, which is what you want
before you claim that a rerun reproduced a file.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Task | Code | Guards against |
|---|---|---|
| Read for discovery | `read_csv(f, col_types = cols(.default = col_character()), na = character())` | Codes converted before you have seen them |
| Tabulate codes | `count(df, site, sex)` | Unseen spellings and conventions |
| Normalize labels | `str_to_title(str_squish(site))` | Fifteen spellings of five sites |
| Restore leading zeros | `str_pad(id, width = 4, pad = "0")` | Keys that match nothing |
| Clean a header | `janitor::clean_names(df)` | Spaces and units in column names |
| Recode by codebook | `case_when(x %in% c("F", "f") ~ "F", ...)` with no `.default` | New codes absorbed silently |
| Name missing codes | `parse_double(x, na = c("", "NA", "-99"))` | Missing codes treated as data |
| Assert ranges | `stopifnot(all(between(x, lo, hi), na.rm = TRUE))` | Implausible values passing through |
| Long to wide | `pivot_wider(names_from = test_code, values_from = value)` | Per-patient conditions computed across rows |
| Wide to long | `pivot_longer(cols, names_to = "variable", values_to = "value")` | Variables hidden in column names |
| Find pivot duplicates | `count(df, id, key) \|> filter(n > 1)` | List-columns and invented values |
| Group without `group_by()` | `summarize(m = median(x), .by = site)` | Groupings left on by accident |
| Count each exclusion | one `filter()` per rule, `nrow()` after each | Unreported subsets |
| Save derived data | `write_rds(df, file.path(derived_dir, "x.rds"))` | Overwritten raw data; lost types |

: Verbs and shapes, with what each guards against.
{#tbl-wrangling-cheat-sheet}

## Further reading

- [@wickham2023r4ds] Chapters 3, 5, and 7, the single-table verbs,
  tidying, and data import.
- [@wickham2014tidy], the original *Tidy Data* paper and the three
  rules.
- [@harrell2025bbr] Chapter 18, 'Information Loss', on why the
  `cut()` in the worked example belongs to the table and not to
  the model.

## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-13}

1. Tidy data satisfy three rules: each variable forms a column,
   each observation forms a row, and each type of observational
   unit forms a table. A typical wide clinical layout has one row
   per patient and one column per variable and time point
   (`sbp_v1`, `sbp_v2`), which breaks the first two: visit is a
   variable hidden in the column names, and one row holds several
   observations.
2. `crf |> filter(ef_pct < 40) |> summarize(mean_sbp = mean(sbp_discharge, na.rm = TRUE), .by = site)`.
   On the raw export this is only correct after the missing-value
   codes have been converted to `NA`, which is the point of this
   chapter's first section.
3. `pivot_longer()` reshapes wide to long: column names become
   values of a new column. Use it when columns encode a variable,
   such as visit, that should be a column of its own, for example
   to plot a trajectory. Use `pivot_wider()` when a calculation
   needs several values for the same unit in one row, such as a
   change from discharge to day 30 or a condition that combines
   two lab tests.
